● Unit Circle Trigonometry

One circle. Every triangle you'll ever need.

Trigonometry looks like a wall of formulas until you meet the idea underneath all of it: a point walking around a circle of radius 1. Once you can see that point, sine and cosine stop being things you memorise — they're just where the point is.

01 · Getting oriented

What is the unit circle?

Everything in this lesson happens on one specific circle. Nail down what it is before anything else.

📐 Definition

The unit circle is the circle of radius 1, centred at the origin, in the $xy$-plane. Its equation is

$$x^2+y^2=1$$

Any point $(x,y)$ that satisfies $x^2+y^2=1$ sits somewhere on this circle — no matter how it's dressed up with square roots and fractions.

✏️ Try it — Question 1

Is the point $\left(\dfrac{\sqrt3}{3}, \dfrac{\sqrt6}{3}\right)$ on the unit circle?

$\left(\dfrac{\sqrt3}{3}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{\sqrt6}{3}\right)^2 = \dfrac{3}{9}+\dfrac{6}{9} = \dfrac{9}{9}=1$ ✓ — it lies exactly on the circle.

✏️ Try it — Question 2

The point $\left(\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}, y\right)$ lies on the unit circle, in Quadrant IV. What is $y$?

STEP 1 — Substitute into $x^2+y^2=1$: $\dfrac{3}{4}+y^2=1 \Rightarrow y^2=\dfrac14$.
STEP 2 — So $y=\pm\dfrac12$. Quadrant IV means $x>0$ and $y<0$, so we keep the negative root.
ANSWER — $y=-\dfrac12$.
02 · A point that walks

Terminal points

The unit circle becomes interesting the moment you let a point move along it.

📐 Definition

Let $t$ be any real number. Starting at $(1,0)$, walk a distance $t$ along the unit circle — counterclockwise if $t>0$, clockwise if $t<0$. Wherever you land is the terminal point $P(x,y)$ determined by $t$.

💡 Key idea

Because the circle has radius 1, "distance walked" and "angle swept" turn out to be the same number, measured in radians. That's the whole reason radians exist — they let arc length double as angle measure. Recall the formula for arc length (s) given a radius (r) and an angle $(\theta)$ is: $s=r\theta.$

03 · Landmarks on the trip

Walking all the way around

The circumference of the unit circle is $2\pi$. That single fact locates four easy landmarks immediately.

Keep walking past a full turn, or start walking backwards, and the same landmarks reappear:

✏️ Quick check

Which direction does the terminal point move when $t=-\dfrac{\pi}{2}$?

04 · The three angles worth memorising

Finding the special terminal points

Only three non-trivial terminal points ever need to be derived by hand: $\pi/4$, $\pi/6$, and $\pi/3$. Every other "nice" angle is a mirror image of one of these. Work through each derivation below.

t = π/4 (45°) — the diagonal

At $\pi/4$, the point is exactly as far from $(1,0)$ as it is from $(0,1)$ along the circle — so by symmetry, $x=y$.

STEP 1 — Since $x=y$, substitute into $x^2+y^2=1$: $x^2+x^2=1 \Rightarrow 2x^2=1$.
STEP 2 — $x = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} = \dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$, and since $x>0,y>0$ here, $y=x$ too.
ANSWER — Terminal point at $t=\pi/4$ is $\left(\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2},\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)$.

t = π/6 (30°) — half an equilateral triangle

Reflect the terminal point at $\pi/6$ across the $x$-axis. The two radii plus the vertical chord between them form an equilateral triangle.

STEP 1 — All three angles of the small triangle are equal (each 60°), so all three sides are equal too — each has length 1 (the radius).
STEP 2 — The vertical side has length $2y$, and it equals 1, so $2y=1 \Rightarrow y=\dfrac12$.
STEP 3 — From $x^2+y^2=1$: $x^2 = 1-\dfrac14=\dfrac34 \Rightarrow x=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$.
ANSWER — Terminal point at $t=\pi/6$ is $\left(\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2},\dfrac12\right)$.

🤔 Why can we say "the vertical side has length exactly $2y$"?

t = π/3 (60°) — a full equilateral triangle

This time build the equilateral triangle directly, using the radius to $(1,0)$ as one side.

STEP 1 — Angle $A$ is 60°. Draw angle $ABC=60°$ too; since angles in a triangle sum to 180°, angle $C$ is also 60° — triangle $ABC$ is equilateral.
STEP 2 — One side of that triangle is the radius, length 1 — so every side is length 1, including the base, which equals $2x$.
STEP 3 — $2x=1 \Rightarrow x=\dfrac12$. Then $y^2=1-\dfrac14=\dfrac34 \Rightarrow y=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$.
ANSWER — Terminal point at $t=\pi/3$ is $\left(\dfrac12,\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)$.

🎯 Spot the pattern

Notice $\pi/6$ gives $\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2},\frac12\right)$ and $\pi/3$ gives $\left(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)$ — the coordinates simply swap. That's because $\pi/6$ and $\pi/3$ are complementary angles ($\pi/6+\pi/3=\pi/2$), and swapping $x\leftrightarrow y$ is exactly what reflecting across the line $y=x$ does.

05 · Naming what the point does

Defining the trigonometric functions

Once you know the terminal point $P(x,y)$ for a given $t$, every trig function is just a name for one of its coordinates (or a ratio of them).

📐 Definition

Let $P(x,y)$ be the terminal point on the unit circle determined by $t$.

$\sin t = y \qquad \cos t = x \qquad \tan t = \dfrac{y}{x}\ (x\ne0)$

$\csc t = \dfrac1y\ (y\ne0) \qquad \sec t = \dfrac1x\ (x\ne0) \qquad \cot t = \dfrac{x}{y}\ (y\ne0)$

🎯 "All Students Take Calculus"

Reading counterclockwise from Quadrant I: All functions positive → Sine (and cosecant) positive → Tangent (and cotangent) positive → Cosine (and secant) positive. Everything else in that quadrant is negative.

✏️ Quick check

In Quadrant III, $x<0$ and $y<0$. Which function is positive there?

$\tan t = y/x$. In Quadrant III both $x$ and $y$ are negative, so their ratio is positive — a negative divided by a negative.
06 · Two languages, one circle

Degrees, radians, and (cos θ, sin θ)

The same twelve landmark points get labelled two different ways depending on which unit you're using — and there's a compact way to write the coordinates themselves.

Because $\cos t$ IS the $x$-coordinate and $\sin t$ IS the $y$-coordinate, every terminal point can be written directly as $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ — no separate lookup needed.

07 · A memory device

The √n/2 pattern

Here's a trick that turns five "different" answers into one formula you can reconstruct in seconds.

🎯 How it works

Along the first quadrant, from $0$ to $\pi/2$, the $x$-coordinates are $\dfrac{\sqrt4}{2}, \dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}, \dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}, \dfrac{\sqrt1}{2}, \dfrac{\sqrt0}{2}$ — the number under the root just counts down from 4 to 0. Simplify each and you get the familiar list: $1, \frac{\sqrt3}{2}, \frac{\sqrt2}{2}, \frac12, 0$. The $y$-coordinates are the same list read backwards.

✏️ Use the pattern

Using the √n/2 trick, what is $\cos(\pi/2)$?

08 · Putting it together

Reading any point on the circle

Once you know the first-quadrant values, every other quadrant is just a sign change — the reference triangle never changes shape, only its position.

STEP 1 — $150° = 180°-30°$, so the reference angle is 30°, whose triangle gives magnitudes $\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2},\frac12\right)$.
STEP 2 — $150°$ lands in Quadrant II, where $x<0, y>0$.
ANSWER — Terminal point: $\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2},\dfrac12\right)$.

✏️ Your turn

Find the terminal point at $t=210°$. (Reference angle: 30°. Which quadrant is 210° in?)

$210°=180°+30°$ → reference angle 30° → Quadrant III, where both coordinates are negative → $\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2},-\dfrac12\right)$.

10 · Self-check

How well does it stick?

Three tiers — recall, apply, and stretch. Try all three before you check the poster above.

Part A · Recall

What is the terminal point for $t=\pi$?

Part B · Apply

Evaluate $\sec(\pi/3)$.

$\cos(\pi/3)=\dfrac12$, and $\sec t = \dfrac1{\cos t}$, so $\sec(\pi/3)=\dfrac{1}{1/2}=2$.

Part C · Stretch

For which values of $t$ in $[0,2\pi)$ is $\sin t = \dfrac12$?

$\sin t=\frac12$ first happens at $t=\pi/6$ (Quadrant I). Sine is also positive in Quadrant II, at the mirror angle $\pi-\pi/6=5\pi/6$. Those are the only two solutions in $[0,2\pi)$.
